metadata.note: PART 2 of 2. Companion to weekly_updates/08-14(2)/ ('From The Crawl To The Conversation'), which covered the BUILD half of the author's LLM-lifecycle blog post. This reel is the DEPLOYMENT half that was deliberately dropped there to hold ~120s: inference knobs, quantization, LoRA/QLoRA, and choosing a model by cheapest cost per successful task. Together the two reels cover the whole post. THROUGH-LINE: everything after training is a cost decision — memory, latency, dollars — and the discipline is to buy capability only where it changes the answer. DOUBLE-CHECK LAW: every figure is the author's own — 7B at 32-bit = 28 GB, half precision 14 GB, INT8 7 GB, INT4 3.5 GB, error per value ~1e-7 to ~1e-1, asymmetric scale = (x_max - x_min) / (q_max - q_min), LoRA W' = W + BA with B of d×r and A of r×k, the 3×3 rank-1 example giving 6 trainable numbers instead of 9, QLoRA = adapters on a frozen 4-bit base putting 7B fine-tuning on one consumer GPU, output tokens several times the price of input tokens, a naive N-step agentic loop growing roughly quadratically. NOTHING is invented. B04's counts (9 and 6) are DERIVED by the component from d/k/r rather than passed in, so the numbers cannot contradict the matrices drawn beside them. B02 uses ScaleComparison, which is a numeric pattern — legitimate here because all four memory values are real; the band is labelled only for the 4-bit case the blog actually makes a claim about. ILLUSTRATE LAW: Claude UI at B00, B07, B08, B09 only; the six body beats are InferenceKnobs -> ScaleComparison -> BinaryBranch -> LoraFactorization -> DivergentFates -> ChipGrid, all distinct. NEW TEMPLATES: LlmInferenceKnobs and LlmLoraFactorization (runtime/remotion/src/LlmDeployIllu.tsx). BRANDING RULE 7: slot-1 kicker stays 'Computational Skepticism'.

beats.narration_text: Training a model and running one are different problems. The first is about capability; the second is almost entirely about cost — memory, latency, and dollars. This is Sai. Here is the half that ships.

props.segment: From The Model To The Bill
props.command: Last time we walked the build: crawl, tokens, attention, fine-tune, reinforcement. Now do the other half — what it takes to actually run one. Precision, adapters, and how to choose a model without just picking the cheapest. Give me the discipline, not the vendor pitch.
output: part two — the build half was the last reel; this is what it costs to ship
precision decides whether it fits; adapters decide what teaching costs
the cheapest model is rarely the cheapest cost per successful task

beats.narration_text: Two knobs matter at inference. Temperature sets how sharply you sample: low is deterministic, high is creative and less reliable. Reasoning effort is misread as a model switch. It is really a budget — the same model, given more room.

show.event: the temperature track appears with both ends labelled
the marker sweeps the range, then settles — a position, not a right answer
the reasoning-effort budget opens along the same width
the steps it buys appear inside it: decompose, try, check, verify
the note lands in terracotta: the same model, given more room

props.effortNote: The same model, given more room.
props.caption: Non-reasoning answers earn their speed on writing, summarization and straightforward code.

beats.narration_text: Deployability is largely a question of precision. As thirty-two-bit floats, a seven-billion-parameter model is twenty-eight gigabytes. Half precision halves it; int eight reaches seven gigabytes, int four, three and a half.

show.event: the log axis draws in, in gigabytes
the 4-bit band shades — the only size the blog claims fits one consumer GPU
FP32 lands at 28 GB
FP16 at 14, INT8 at 7
INT4 lands hot at 3.5 GB, inside the band

data.slideMeta: PRECISION · A 7B MODEL IN MEMORY · ERROR PER VALUE GROWS ~1e-7 → ~1e-1

beats.narration_text: Quantization can be symmetric, or asymmetric — carrying a zero point alongside a scale. And it can be applied after training with a calibration pass, or during it, so the model learns to tolerate the coarser grid.

show.event: the question node: how do you map the weights onto a coarser grid?
two branches draw down — symmetric on one side, asymmetric on the other
each card carries what it costs you
the ghost line surfaces: the grid is coarser either way
the resolver lands in terracotta — after training, or during it

branches.fix: one scale factor, and nothing else to carry

beats.narration_text: LoRA attacks the other cost: full fine-tuning updates every weight. Freeze the original matrix, and learn the update as a product of two thin ones. QLoRA trains those adapters on a frozen four-bit base.

show.event: W appears as a grey 3×3 grid, frozen
the plus sign lands
B and A appear beside it in terracotta — a tall sliver and a wide one
the full fine-tune cost counts out: nine cells, all trainable
the rank-1 cost counts out beneath it: six
the QLoRA footnote lands

props.sparkLine: Learn the update, not the weights.
props.rankNote: rank r — the dial between adaptation capacity and cost
props.footnote: QLoRA: the same adapters, on a frozen 4-bit base.
props.caption: At real scale the ratio is orders of magnitude, not nine to six.

beats.narration_text: In production the harder question is which model to run. The answer is not the cheapest model, but the cheapest cost per successful task — tokens, plus retries, tool calls, latency, and the cost of being wrong.

the split marker: how do you pick the model?
the cheapest-sticker track bends down — retries and repairs eat the saving
the weakest-that-works track climbs
both endpoints badge: lowest sticker, versus lowest cost per success

beats.narration_text: Output tokens cost several times input tokens, and dominate latency. Input tokens are cheap individually, but explode in agentic systems, where a naive N-step loop grows roughly quadratically. Token cuts that quietly cost accuracy are a false economy.

show.event: the levers snap into the grid one at a time
each dot lights terracotta as its chip settles
caption lands: the quadratic warning for agentic loops

props.caption: A naive N-step agentic loop grows roughly quadratically in input tokens.

beats.narration_text: The second half on one page. Precision decides whether it fits. LoRA decides what it costs to teach. The model you pick decides the bill. Ask what the weakest model is that works reliably — and answer that on your own eval set.

line 3 (LoRA and QLoRA)
line 4 (cost per successful task) lands

props.artifactTitle: From The Model To The Bill
artifactLines: Reasoning effort is a budget, not a model switch. The extra thinking earns its latency on algorithm design, debugging and long multi-step work — and not on writing or straightforward code.
Precision decides whether it fits: a 7B model is 28 GB at 32-bit, 14 at half, 7 at INT8, 3.5 at INT4, with the error per value growing from about 1e-7 to 1e-1 along the way.
LoRA freezes W and learns the update as B times A, so a 3×3 layer at rank 1 trains 6 numbers instead of 9. QLoRA stacks that on a frozen 4-bit base — 7B fine-tuning on one consumer GPU.
In production, buy the cheapest cost per SUCCESSFUL task, not the cheapest token. Reach for classical ML when the task is a pattern over well-defined features, and an LLM when it is unstructured.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take one task you run often. Price it end to end — tokens, retries, tool calls — then run it again on the weakest model that might work. Compare on your own examples.

props.command: Take one task I run often. Price it end to end — input tokens, output tokens, retries, tool calls, latency. Now run the same task on the weakest model that might plausibly work, score both on twenty of my own examples, and tell me the cost per SUCCESSFUL task for each.

beats.narration_text: From the model to the bill. This lifecycle has been stable for years, while every stage inside it keeps moving. From Andrej Karpathy's deep dive. Sai.
